name: Jaw implants

lead: Jaw implants, also called mandibular angle or gonial implants, are solid shapes of silicone, porous polyethylene or PEEK placed over the lower jawbone. People want them for a wider, more defined, squarer lower face.

The implant sits against the bone under the soft tissue, so the contour of the jaw looks wider at the angle and body. In published literature they appear mainly in facial gender-affirming surgery, where mandibular angle and body augmentation is described as a masculinising option, with one review reporting minimal complications and stating that more outcome research is needed.

paras: Placement is usually through an incision inside the mouth. Some designs are custom-made from CT scans. Forum users compare implants with bimax and genioplasty and talk about implant size, body fat and whether the underlying structure suits an implant. Swelling settles over weeks.

Reported concerns include a bloated or unnatural look when implants are too large or the structure is mismatched, soft-tissue sagging after removal, infection and displacement. Outcome data on cosmetic jaw implants are limited. They are placed by a surgeon under anaesthesia.

angle.text: Jaw implants add width and definition at the angle and body of the lower jaw, giving a squarer, sharper outline that shows once swelling settles. They are used in facial gender surgery and cosmetic work, and reviews note more outcome research is needed.

lead: Jaw implants are manufactured shapes, usually of silicone or porous polyethylene, placed against the outer surface of the lower jaw (the mandible) to add width, squareness and definition to the lower face. They are also called mandibular angle, gonial angle or jawline implants.[1][2] People who want a stronger or wider jawline use them to change the outline of the lower face without cutting the jawbone, and they are often paired with a chin implant or a sliding genioplasty so that chin and jaw read as one continuous contour.[3]

The procedure has a clinical literature of its own, which describes two basic implant types for aesthetic augmentation of the jaw angles, standard and custom, and discusses technique and ways to avoid common complications.[2] A prospective study of 116 solid silicone implants reported low infection rates and high patient satisfaction, while a case series of implant movement and muscle displacement has urged surgeons to preserve the soft-tissue sling around the angle of the jaw.[2] The best-known related setting is facial gender-affirming surgery, where a review of lower jaw recontouring describes reducing or augmenting the angle, body and chin and reports minimal complications.[1]

On looksmax.org, jaw implants are discussed as a lower-downtime alternative or complement to bone surgery such as bimaxillary surgery, with long-running debates about implant design, size, body fat and whether the underlying skeleton suits an implant.[4] Published outcome research on cosmetic jaw implants remains small, and much of the discussion rests on individual before-and-after reports.[2]

paras: A jaw implant is a solid or semi-solid shape that sits against the outer surface of the lower jawbone. Different designs target the gonial angle at the back corner of the jaw, the body along the side, or an extended shape that wraps both; some are made as custom pieces from CT scans of the individual patient.[2] Surgeons usually place them through an incision inside the mouth so that there is no visible scar, creating a pocket over the bone for the implant.[3]

A 2019 review of mandibular angle implants by the surgeon Barry Eppley describes the two basic types of implant used for aesthetic augmentation of the jaw angles, the goals of augmentation, how the implants are placed with attention to avoiding common complications, and when standard versus custom implants are indicated.[2]

The anatomical logic is that a wider, sharper lower face reads as more masculine or more defined. An overview of facial feminisation surgery notes that male jawlines extend from the chin at a wider angle and end in a sharper corner at the back than female jawlines, and that chins in men tend to be longer, wider and squarer.[5] Many looksmaxxing discussions of the jawline use the same vocabulary of angle, width and squareness.

Materials discussed for chin implants, which forum users apply by analogy to jaw implants, include silicone, which is smooth and flexible, does not bond to tissue and is easy to remove; porous polyethylene (Medpor), into which tissue grows, anchoring it and helping resist infection but making removal harder; and ePTFE, which is flexible, porous and held with titanium screws.[3] Wikipedia notes that silicone can shift or buckle and, in some cases, cause bone resorption where it contacts the mandible.[3]

For the jaw angle specifically, a 1996 report from oral and maxillofacial surgeons described a large-pore polyethylene implant used in patients with severe facial deformities and previous surgery, presenting four cases with very satisfactory aesthetic results and recommending the approach when indications are strictly observed.[2] Later series have concentrated on solid silicone.

Bone-based approaches include orthognathic (corrective jaw) surgery, in which the upper jaw, lower jaw or both are cut, moved and fixed; it is mainly used for bite and jaw-structure problems and can also be considered for aesthetics, with software used to predict the post-operative appearance.[6] Sliding genioplasty cuts a horseshoe-shaped piece from the lower chin border and moves it forward or back, fixing it with a plate and screws.[3] Non-surgical options for the lower face include hyaluronic acid or calcium hydroxyapatite fillers, which are temporary, while permanent free silicone injections have fallen out of favour because of migration and inflammation.[3]

Facial gender-affirming literature treats jaw work as one element of a package that may include the chin, cheeks and forehead. Wikipedia reports that the jaw can be reshaped by reduction surgery through the mouth and that the masseter muscle can be reduced to make the jaw look narrower, and that surgeons began developing the field in the early 1980s, notably Douglas Ousterhout after a request in 1982.[5]

A review of lower jaw recontouring in facial gender-affirming surgery describes augmentation of the angle, body and chin with implants, fat or bone, reports minimal complications and says more outcome research is needed.[1]

A prospective study from Al-Jandan and Marei, published in 2018, followed 58 patients (56 women and 2 men) who received bilateral solid silicone mandibular angle implants, 116 implants in all, for at least six months. In the abstract, 96 implants had no complications, 5 (4.3 percent) became infected and 16 (13.8 percent) were displaced, and three patients without complications (6 percent) were dissatisfied with their final appearance. The authors concluded that infection and displacement rates were low and satisfaction high.[7][2]

A 2010 report by Bastidas and Zide, titled 'The treachery of mandibular angle augmentation', described five patients with complications after angle augmentation with silicone or porous implants, including implant movement and displacement of the masseter muscle, one of which needed revision through a modified Risdon approach. The authors advocated maintaining the pterygomasseteric sling during placement.[2]

A retrospective CT study of cosmetic-surgery foreign bodies in the maxillofacial region catalogued how such materials appear on imaging as incidental findings and did not assess outcomes.[8] Dental, corticobasal or subperiosteal jaw implants, such as 3D-printed titanium frameworks for tooth replacement, address chewing function in people with bone loss and are a separate field from cosmetic contouring.[9]

General risks described for chin and jaw implants include swelling, haematoma and temporary lip numbness or weakness, with less common problems such as infection, implant displacement, bony changes and nerve injury; surgeon experience is described as reducing these.[3] Bone-cutting procedures in facial feminisation list injury to the mental nerve, damage to tooth roots, infection and non-union.[5] Orthognathic surgery is reported to carry infection rates of up to 7 percent and temporary numbness that usually recovers within about three months, with rare permanent nerve damage.[6]
Forum users add concerns specific to appearance: an implant that is too large or does not fit the underlying bone can look bloated, and removal may not return the soft tissue to its earlier state.[4]

Jaw implants are a regular topic on looksmax.org, where threads compare them with bimaxillary surgery, ask whether a given face is a suitable candidate, share early post-operative photos and discuss surgeons and travel for surgery.[4] Participants frequently argue over whether disappointing results come from implant design or from the size chosen, with some advocating more conservative augmentation.[4]

One thread asks whether being heavier at the time of surgery changes the final look and whether leaning down later resolves it; one reply states that a short or recessed mandible can make an implant on the side look bloated.[4] These are community opinions rather than published findings.

lore.intro: Jaw implants are discussed on forums as a way to widen or define the lower face, with recurring debates about design versus size, about which skeletal structures suit an implant, and about how they compare with bimaxillary surgery.[4]

claims.claim: Being a little overweight at the time of surgery does not change the final implant result once weight is lost.
Jaw implants look bloated or unnatural on people with a short or recessed mandible.
Poor jaw implant results usually come from oversizing rather than from implants as a concept.
Implants are a cheaper, lower-downtime route to a stronger jawline than bone surgery.
Silicone implants are low-risk once placed correctly.
Porous polyethylene anchors better than silicone, but is harder to remove if the result disappoints.

timeline.event: Simon Hullihen publishes one of the first cases in what becomes orthognathic jaw surgery.[6]
Jaw osteotomies develop; Hugo Obwegeser later popularises the bilateral sagittal split osteotomy.[6]
Douglas Ousterhout is asked to operate on a trans woman patient, beginning his development of facial feminisation procedures including jaw and chin work.[5]
Surgeons report large-pore polyethylene implants for mandibular angle augmentation in patients with severe deformities.[2]
Bastidas and Zide report five cases of complications after angle augmentation and urge preservation of the pterygomasseteric sling.[2]
A prospective series of 116 solid silicone angle implants reports 4.3 percent infection and 13.8 percent displacement.[7][2]
Reviews of mandibular angle implants and of lower jaw recontouring in facial gender-affirming surgery are published.[1][2]
